Under unified government or intense polarization, a large supermajority can still be assembled along partisan lines—or, just as destabilizing, the process itself can be weaponized even when conviction is unlikely.

II. How the Current Threshold Encourages Politicization

The problem is not only that removal might occur on partisan grounds. It is that the very threat and use of impeachment are becoming normalized and politicized. Several structural dynamics drive this:

  1. Impeachment as political theater. When the Senate threshold is perceived as achievable or at least plausibly in play, a narrowly partisan House majority has every incentive to initiate impeachment even if it is virtually certain to fail. The process itself—the hearings, media coverage, and public branding—becomes the goal. Removal is almost beside the point. This erodes the norm that impeachment should be reserved for truly extraordinary, broadly recognized misconduct.

  2. Retaliatory escalation. Once one party has used impeachment aggressively, the other party feels justified in responding in kind when it regains power. Over time, the practice spirals: each side cites prior impeachments as precedent and cover. A two‑thirds threshold that might have constrained impulsive majorities in the 18th century does not effectively block this logic in a hardened two‑party system.

  3. Chronic uncertainty and instability. A President, judge, or cabinet officer who governs under constant impeachment threats is not just personally vulnerable; the entire branch’s stability is undermined. Markets, foreign governments, and domestic agencies all must treat the possibility of removal as part of the normal political environment. The office becomes less about its constitutional function and more about surviving legislative siege.

  4. Erosion of the separation of powers. When impeachment is easy to deploy—even unsuccessfully—it becomes a tool for the legislative branch to exert day‑to‑day pressure on the executive and judiciary. That distorts the intended equilibrium. The result is less an independent executive and judiciary, and more a government where every decision is litigated through the lens of “Will this trigger impeachment?” rather than “Is this lawful and constitutional?”

A higher threshold would not eliminate partisanship, but it would sharply change the calculus. Making removal clearly and consistently unattainable without a broad, cross‑party consensus would remove much of the strategic appeal of launching dubious impeachments in the first place.

III. Why Raising the Threshold Would Improve Constitutional Governance

Strengthening the removal threshold would deliver several concrete benefits.

1. It would restore impeachment’s status as a last resort.

If conviction required, say, three‑quarters of the Senate—or a comparable supermajority of both chambers—a party could not realistically treat impeachment as a routine, symbolic gesture. The public would quickly recognize that any impeachment effort lacking support across the political spectrum was fundamentally unserious.

That would powerfully reinforce the norm that impeachment is reserved for the rare, catastrophic case where a federal official’s conduct is so egregious that nearly everyone—across party and ideology—agrees they can no longer serve. That is what makes impeachment legitimate: not just legality, but broad legitimacy grounded in shared judgment.

2. It would reduce incentives for purely partisan impeachments.

Today, launching an impeachment can be politically useful even if conviction is impossible, because the process inflicts reputational damage and energizes a party’s base. Raising the removal bar would blunt that incentive.

If everyone knows that conviction is impossible without substantial support from the other party—and that the other party has firmly signaled opposition from the outset—then a majority’s attempt to impeach looks nakedly partisan and performative. That increases the political cost of frivolous impeachments, as swing voters and institutionalists recoil from transparent abuse of a grave constitutional mechanism.

By contrast, when the threshold is relatively lower, partisans can persuade themselves—and their voters—that removal is at least theoretically attainable, preserving the illusion that the endeavor is a genuine effort to protect the republic rather than a political campaign by other means.

3. It would reinforce electoral accountability as the primary remedy.

The American system is designed on the premise that, in general, officials—especially Presidents—are held accountable by the electorate on a regular schedule. Impeachment is an extraordinary exception to that rule, justified only when allowing an official to serve out the remainder of a term is plainly intolerable.

By raising the threshold, the constitutional architecture would once again reflect that elections, not legislative punishment, are the main vehicle for accountability. Voters and parties would be forced to take elections more seriously as the decisive moment to accept or reject an incumbent’s conduct, rather than treating Congress as a standing recall commission.

This aligns with democratic principles: the people, not politicians, ordinarily decide who governs.

4. It would better protect the independence of the judiciary and executive.

Federal judges enjoy life tenure precisely to shield them from political pressure. Cabinet officers and other executive-branch officials are appointed through a process designed to give them enough security to carry out their duties lawfully even when their actions are politically controversial.

An impeachment process easily weaponized undermines that security. Raising the removal threshold would not make judges or executive officers unaccountable; it would make them accountable for truly serious misconduct, not for unpopular decisions. This is especially critical for judges, whose constitutional duty is to interpret law, not to mirror transient majority opinion.

5. It would align the process with the gravity of the penalty.

Removal by impeachment is an extreme remedy. It overturns the choice of the electorate (for elected officials) or the deliberate appointment process (for judges and officers) and permanently brands the removed official with a unique constitutional stigma. It can trigger cascading institutional disruption, including leadership crises in the executive, reconfiguration of the judiciary, and broader political instability.

For penalties of similar magnitude elsewhere in the constitutional order, the Framers typically demanded the highest procedural safeguards and supermajorities. As the political system has evolved, it has become clear that a two‑thirds requirement, though substantial, is not as extreme a safeguard in practice as it appears on paper. Increasing it would better reflect the existential nature of the penalty.

IV. Addressing the Obvious Objection: What About Truly Dangerous Officials?

The main objection to raising the threshold is straightforward: making removal harder could allow genuinely dangerous or corrupt officials to remain in office when they should not.

That concern is serious—but it is overstated, for several reasons.

  1. Other constitutional and legal mechanisms exist. For Presidents, the 25th Amendment provides a mechanism for temporary or permanent removal in cases of incapacity. Criminal law remains available both during and after service. Elections offer regular opportunities for peaceful replacement. For other federal officers, resignation under pressure, internal disciplinary procedures, and criminal prosecution all mitigate the risk of impunity.

  2. Truly catastrophic misconduct tends to produce bipartisan consensus. The scenarios most often invoked—open defiance of court orders, egregious corruption, clear-cut abuse of power—are precisely those in which the political costs of defending the official become untenable across party lines. When a President or judge has plainly crossed that line, even loyalists have strong incentives to abandon them. A higher threshold in such cases would likely still be reachable.

  3. The greater danger is routine, partisan use of impeachment, not its underuse. Historically, and especially in recent decades, the problem has not been a shortage of mechanisms to remove manifestly unfit officials, but an increasing willingness to drag the country through impeachment battles over heavily contested or partisan issues. This chronic stress weakens institutions over time, erodes public trust, and teaches each generation that constitutional norms are malleable tools of political expediency.

  4. A higher threshold would force Congress to build real, broad cases. If removal required a towering supermajority, Congress could not rely on partisan momentum or a narrow media narrative. It would have to investigate more thoroughly, build a more compelling factual record, and persuade the country across ideological lines. That makes wrongful removal less likely and ensures that removal, when it happens, rests on a far more solid foundation.

It is better, in a constitutional democracy, to tolerate some risk that a flawed official will finish a term than to normalize a process in which officials are regularly threatened with removal by their partisan opponents. Stability and predictability are not luxuries; they are preconditions for the rule of law.

V. How This Change Could Be Structured

There are many ways to implement a higher threshold while preserving constitutional flexibility. For example:

  • Require three‑quarters of the Senate to convict.
  • Require a two‑thirds vote of the entire membership of both House and Senate, not just those present.
  • Require concurrence between branches, such as a supermajority in the Senate plus a confirming supermajority of the Supreme Court (on the legal sufficiency of the charges, not the facts).

Any of these would be a major improvement over the status quo. The precise design is less important than the principle: removal should be possible only with overwhelming, cross‑partisan agreement.

Yes, these changes would require a constitutional amendment—a high bar. But that is appropriate. Adjusting the rules governing how the people’s chosen leaders can be forcibly removed from power is among the most fundamental decisions a polity can make. The amendment process ensures that such reforms themselves enjoy broad, cross‑regional, and bipartisan support.

Conclusion

Impeachment is too powerful a tool to be left vulnerable to routine partisan exploitation. The combination of modern polarization, permanent campaigning, and media-driven politics has eroded the practical safeguards the Framers thought they were building into the process. A two‑thirds Senate threshold, once a formidable obstacle, no longer reliably prevents impeachment from being used as a political cudgel rather than a constitutional safeguard.

Raising the threshold for removal would not eliminate partisanship, nor would it render genuinely dangerous officials untouchable. Instead, it would push impeachment back into the narrow space for which it was originally intended: a rare, last‑ditch remedy reserved for the most egregious and widely recognized betrayals of public trust.

A republic that removes its leaders too easily risks becoming unstable and vengeful; one that removes them only when nearly everyone agrees they must go is far more likely to be restrained, predictable, and just. By making impeachment harder, the United States would make its constitutional order stronger.

Core idea: Frequent or easily triggered impeachment efforts can destabilize governance, markets, and foreign policy.

  • Avoiding “normalization” of removal:
    If impeachment were used routinely, its power as a deterrent against genuine abuse might paradoxically diminish; officials might treat impeachment threats as political noise. Higher bars keep the remedy rare and therefore more feared by those tempted toward serious misconduct.

Core idea: When removal is hard, parties and institutions must take more responsibility up front.

  • Better record for the public and history:
    More elaborate procedures tend to generate detailed factual records, committee reports, and debate transcripts. This helps the public evaluate the legitimacy of the process and constrains future misuse by setting precedents.

8. Preventing Cycles of Retaliation

Core idea: If impeachment is easy, each party may feel justified in retaliating when it gains power, creating a destructive cycle.

  • Breaking “tit-for-tat” dynamics:
    Once one side uses impeachment aggressively, the other may respond in kind. A high constitutional and procedural bar makes it harder to escalate that cycle because succeeding in impeachment still requires broad agreement, not just control of one chamber.

  • Protecting minority parties and future majorities alike:
    Parties are sometimes in the majority and sometimes in the minority. Strong impeachment barriers protect all parties from the temptation to set precedents that will later be used against them.

Core idea: Judges are especially vulnerable to retaliation because their decisions naturally create winners and losers.

  • Shielding legal decision-making from political swings:
    If each new majority in Congress could easily impeach judges whose decisions it dislikes, constitutional rights and legal stability would depend on the political winds. High impeachment hurdles help keep the law more consistent over time.

  • Safeguarding minority rights:
    Courts often protect unpopular minorities or enforce constitutional limits against majority preferences. Making impeachment difficult supports the judiciary’s ability to perform this role without constant fear of removal.

Supporters of higher impeachment thresholds or additional procedural barriers argue that they:

  • Protect the separation of powers and institutional independence.
  • Discourage partisan weaponization and performative impeachments.
  • Reinforce electoral accountability as the primary method of removal.
  • Promote continuity in governance, foreign policy, and markets.
  • Preserve impeachment as a rare, high-gravity constitutional remedy.
  • Encourage better candidate selection and internal checks.
  • Improve due process, fact-finding, and public legitimacy.
  • Reduce cycles of partisan retaliation.
  • Particularly safeguard the judiciary from political retaliation.

All of these arguments are rooted in prioritizing long-term stability and resistance to partisan attacks over short-term political advantage, while still keeping impeachment available for truly egregious abuses of power.

To some, that sounds unbearable. Much easier to keep impeachment as a low-friction, high-drama release valve and call any attempt to tighten standards “authoritarian.”

In Conclusion: Raise the Bar, Lower the Drama

Making impeachment harder isn’t about letting bad officials run wild; it’s about forcing everyone—Congress, media, and voters—to treat removal from office as a last resort, not the first button you press after a disappointing news cycle.

The loudest defenders of the current low bar don’t fear tyranny.

If democracy can’t function without casual, recurring impeachment…
Maybe the problem isn’t the threshold.

My fellow Americans,

We live in a restless age.

News cycles turn by the hour. Outrage is manufactured by the minute. And in the midst of that storm, one of the most solemn powers in our Constitution—the power to impeach and remove federal officials—has drifted dangerously close to becoming just another political weapon.

The Original Design—and How We’ve Drifted

The framers of our Constitution were not naïve. They feared demagogues. They feared corruption. They feared presidents who might abuse power or judges who might become tyrants in robes.

So they created impeachment as a safeguard—a safety valve, not a weapon of choice.

Alexander Hamilton described impeachment as a “national inquest” into the conduct of public men. But he also warned that impeachment proceedings would “agitate the passions of the whole community” and risk turning into contests of party and faction. He trusted that the difficulty, the gravity, and the political cost of impeachment would keep it rare.

For a long time, that was largely true. Impeachments were few, and removals even fewer. The very idea carried a moral and political weight that made leaders hesitate.

But look at where we are today.

Presidents face impeachment threats almost as a matter of routine. Federal judges and executive officials are regularly denounced as impeachable for decisions that some faction finds disagreeable, not unlawful. The word “impeachment” has become a fundraising slogan, a cable-news chyron, a social-media hashtag.

The danger is not simply that we might impeach more often. The deeper danger is that we normalize impeachment—turn it into just another legislative maneuver—until it loses its meaning and fractures the stability of our institutions.

Our Constitution does not need impeachment to be easy. It needs it to be serious.

Raising the bar for impeachment is not about protecting politicians; it is about protecting the rule of law and the continuity of our constitutional system.

We should demand a higher standard for at least three fundamental reasons:

1. Stability is a public good.

A stable government is not a luxury. It is the foundation on which everything else stands: our economy, our national security, our global credibility, and our ability to plan for the future.

When the holders of the highest offices live under constant, credible threat of removal by partisan whim, they govern with one eye on the law and the other on the latest poll or partisan outrage. Decisions become defensive. Long-term thinking is replaced by short-term survival.

We do not want a government that is too afraid to act. We want a government that is constrained by law—but not constantly shaken by partisan upheaval.

2. Elections must mean something.

In our system, the people’s primary check on bad leaders is the ballot box. Impeachment is supposed to be the exception, not the substitute. When impeachment becomes a routine tool of opposition, it effectively allows a slim majority in one chamber of Congress to override the decision of millions of voters.

That does not mean impeachment should never overturn an election—only that doing so must require more than temporary partisan advantage. It should require clear, overwhelming evidence of grave misconduct and broad consensus across party lines that the official cannot remain in office.

If we truly believe in democracy, then we must treat the reversal of an election result as an extraordinary act—not a partisan habit.

3. We should fear the precedent we set—because someday, it will be used against us.

No party, no movement, no ideology holds power forever. The weapons we sharpen today will be turned on us tomorrow.

Those who cheer an easy impeachment process when it threatens a leader they dislike must understand: the same low threshold will be there when their preferred leader faces a hostile Congress. The same loose standards will be used to justify what they will then call “witch hunts,” “persecution,” “criminalization of politics.”

If you care about your principles more than your party, you should want impeachment to be hard—to require such strong evidence and such broad agreement that it is almost never used, and never abused.

The Cost of Politicized Impeachment

We need to be honest about the damage that politicized or low-threshold impeachment inflicts on the republic:

  • It erodes trust in all branches of government. When impeachment looks like a partisan ritual, people stop believing there is such a thing as objective justice in politics.
  • It weakens the separation of powers, tempting Congress to dominate the executive and judicial branches through constant threats of removal.
  • It encourages extremism, because each party knows it can try to topple the other’s leaders instead of persuading voters and winning elections over time.
  • It paralyzes governance, leaving major crises unresolved as all sides focus on survival and retaliation.

The result is not accountability. The result is chaos.

What Raising the Bar Could Look Like

If we are serious about protecting incumbents from partisan abuses of impeachment, we must be serious about changing the structure of the process—not to protect individuals, but to protect the institution.

There are several reforms we should consider:

1. Higher voting thresholds in the House

Right now, a simple majority in the House can approve articles of impeachment. That means a single party can initiate impeachment purely on party-line votes.

We should consider requiring a three-fifths or even two-thirds vote in the House to impeach a president, a cabinet officer, or a federal judge. If a case for removal cannot convince a meaningful portion of the minority party, it may not rise to the level of “high crimes and misdemeanors.”

This would not make impeachment impossible. It would make it bipartisan—forcing evidence and arguments strong enough to transcend party loyalty.

2. Clearer constitutional or statutory standards

“High crimes and misdemeanors” is a phrase that invites interpretation. That flexibility can be wise—but in an age of bitter partisanship, it becomes a vulnerability.

Congress, through statute or rule, could more precisely define:

  • What kinds of conduct truly qualify as impeachable,
  • What evidentiary standards should be met, and
  • What process should be followed before impeachment is even voted upon.

We could, for example, distinguish sharply between:

  • Policy disagreements and abuse of power,
  • Error or negligence and corrupt intent,
  • Unpopular decisions and constitutional violations.

Impeachment should be reserved for the last category—not used to relitigate elections or policy outcomes.

3. Independent inquiry requirements

Before taking the explosive step of impeachment, the House could be required to:

  • Receive findings from an independent, bipartisan commission or special counsel,
  • Conduct formal, public hearings with due process protections,
  • Allow the accused official an opportunity to respond and present a defense.

This would not remove impeachment from Congress’s control, but it would impose a discipline of evidence and procedure, making partisan rushes to impeachment more difficult.

4. Procedural safeguards against repeated or frivolous attempts

We should consider rules that:

  • Limit repeated impeachment attempts on the same official for the same alleged conduct,
  • Require a cooling-off period,
  • Or necessitate additional thresholds before reopening impeachment once it has failed.

We do not allow prosecutors to endlessly retry the same person for the same alleged crime. In the same spirit, we should not allow perpetual impeachment campaigns kept alive for political leverage.

Protecting Incumbents Is Protecting the Office

When we talk about “protecting incumbents,” some people instinctively recoil, as if we are proposing immunity for those in power.

But that is not what this is about.

Protecting incumbents from abusive impeachment is not protecting individuals—it is protecting institutions.

It is protecting:

  • The presidency from becoming a prize that can be nullified whenever the opposition gains the House.
  • The judiciary from becoming a collection of judges constantly under threat for ruling the “wrong” way.
  • The executive branch from being unable to function because its officers are targeted for removal whenever their decisions anger one chamber of Congress.

We already have many mechanisms to hold officials accountable without constantly reaching for impeachment:

  • Criminal investigation and prosecution after leaving office,
  • Oversight hearings,
  • Ethics investigations,
  • Elections and reappointments,
  • Public scrutiny and political pressure.

Impeachment should stand apart from all of these—a constitutional last line of defense, not a first option for those who lost the last election.

Looking Beyond Parties—Thinking as Citizens, Not Partisans

We must be honest: both major parties, at different times and in different ways, have treated impeachment and the threat of impeachment as a tool of partisan warfare.

This is not a story of one side’s guilt and the other’s purity. It is a story of a system that has allowed temptation to flourish and wisdom to fade.

So the solution cannot be to trust one party over the other. The solution is to raise the structural and procedural barriers so that no party, no faction, no moment of anger can easily transform impeachment into a political bludgeon.

This is a call to think as citizens, not partisans.

Ask yourself:

  • Do you want your preferred leaders to govern in constant fear of being toppled by a hostile House on thin, partisan grounds?
  • Do you want major policy disputes to be fought not at the ballot box, but through impeachment hearings?
  • Do you believe that any president, any judge, any official you admire would be safe in a world where impeachment is cheap, easy, and common?

If the answer is no, then you already believe in what I am arguing: impeachment should be hard. Impeachment should be rare. Impeachment should be reserved for the clearest and gravest abuses, proven to an overwhelming share of the nation.

A Stronger Republic Requires Restraint

There is a paradox in republican government: to keep it strong, we must sometimes restrain ourselves.

We are tempted, in moments of frustration or outrage, to demand immediate justice, immediate removal, immediate vindication of our side’s cause. But the Constitution was not written to satisfy our impulses; it was written to restrain them—for the long-term survival of liberty.

Raising the standards and difficulty of impeachment is an act of constitutional humility. It is a way of saying:

We will not use this power lightly. We will not overturn elections casually. We will not destabilize our institutions to win a momentary victory.

We will hold our leaders accountable—but we will do so in ways that preserve the integrity of the offices they hold and the continuity of the government we all depend on.

A Call to Action

If we truly want to protect our democracy, we must protect it from the erosion of its own most powerful tools.

Let us:

  • Call on our representatives to support reforms that require broader consensus for impeachment;
  • Demand clearer standards that distinguish corruption from disagreement;
  • Insist on due process and independent investigation before the gravest step is taken;
  • And reject, loudly and consistently, the casual, partisan invocation of impeachment as a political slogan.

This is not about this president or that judge, this administration or that Congress. This is about the kind of republic we intend to leave to those who come after us.

A republic in which impeachment is a sober shield, used rarely and reluctantly?

Or a republic in which impeachment is a partisan hammer, swung at every opportunity until the structure itself begins to crack?

I choose the first. I choose a system in which impeachment is difficult, rare, and respected—precisely because it is not easily abused.

Let us raise the bar.

Let us protect incumbents from partisan abuse not for their sake, but for ours—for the sake of a stable, durable, self-governing nation.

And let us commit, across parties and ideologies, to the discipline and restraint that a healthy constitutional order demands.

Thank you.

Raising the Bar: Amending the Impeachment Threshold to End Partisan Weaponization and Restore Constitutional Legitimacy

In the summer of 2023, as Republican lawmakers in the U.S. House of Representatives launched a formal impeachment inquiry into President Joe Biden over his administration’s border policy and unproven allegations of family financial impropriety, even conservative legal scholars were forced to confront a grim reality: impeachment, the constitutional process designed as a last-resort safeguard against abuses of public power, had been fully reduced to a partisan political cudgel. For decades, the threat and use of impeachment has been deployed not to punish treason, bribery, or violations of the public trust, but to delegitimize political opponents, energize partisan bases, and reverse electoral outcomes disliked by the opposing party. To restore the process’s original purpose, curb toxic polarization, and protect the integrity of U.S. governance, the Constitution must be amended to drastically raise the threshold for removal of federal officials: requiring a two-thirds supermajority in the House of Representatives to impeach, a three-quarters supermajority in the Senate to convict, and explicitly limiting grounds for impeachment to proven abuses of official duty, excluding policy disagreements and personal misconduct unrelated to public office.

The Framers of the Constitution designed impeachment as a rare, grave check on official misconduct, explicitly built to resist partisan abuse. During the 1787 Constitutional Convention, delegates debated at length how to balance the need to remove corrupt officials with the risk of allowing a temporary congressional majority to overturn the will of the electorate. James Madison, the “Father of the Constitution,” argued that while impeachment was a “capital defect” of the British system that allowed monarchs to act with impunity, its American iteration had to be guarded against factional misuse. In Federalist No. 65, Alexander Hamilton made the Framers’ intent explicit: impeachment was reserved for “those offenses which proceed from the misconduct of public men, or, in other words, from the abuse or violation of some public trust,” and was never meant to address policy disputes or personal failings. To ensure this, the Framers set the Senate conviction threshold at two-thirds of those present—a supermajority deliberately chosen to require broad, bipartisan consensus that removal was necessary. As Hamilton noted, this threshold was intended to prevent impeachment from becoming “the instrument of faction” rather than “the instrument of justice.” The Framers’ design was clear: impeachment was not a tool for political revenge, but a last resort for when an official’s conduct threatened the very integrity of the office they held.

For most of U.S. history, this design functioned as intended. Prior to the 1990s, impeachment inquiries were rare, almost always launched with bipartisan support, and reserved for unambiguous cases of abuse of power. The only two presidents impeached before the 21st century—Andrew Johnson in 1868 and Bill Clinton in 1998—were both products of extreme political polarization, but even these efforts fell short of the Framers’ vision. Johnson’s impeachment was driven by a radical Republican majority furious over his obstruction of Reconstruction policies, and Clinton’s was launched over a personal affair and related perjury, conduct entirely unrelated to his official duties. In both cases, the process consumed months of congressional time, cost tens of millions of dollars, and failed to secure the two-thirds Senate majority required for removal, leaving the public broadly cynical that impeachment was anything more than a partisan stunt. But these were outliers—until the 21st century, when impeachment became a routine feature of partisan warfare.

The modern era of weaponized impeachment began in earnest with the two impeachments of Donald Trump, which cemented the process as a tool of partisan messaging rather than legitimate oversight. Trump’s first impeachment, over his pressure on Ukraine to investigate then-candidate Joe Biden, was passed by the House with only two Democratic defections, and acquitted by the Senate with only one Republican voting to convict—both votes split almost perfectly along party lines. The second impeachment, passed days after the January 6, 2021 Capitol riot for Trump’s role in inciting the insurrection, saw 10 House Republicans break with their party to support impeachment, but the Senate still fell 10 votes short of the two-thirds threshold, with only seven Republicans voting to convict. In both cases, the process was not driven by a desire for accountability, but by partisan calculation: House Democrats used the first impeachment to rally their base ahead of the 2020 election, while Senate Republicans used the acquittals to signal their loyalty to Trump’s base. The effect was devastating: public trust in Congress plummeted, and the impeachment process came to be seen by large swathes of the public as nothing more than a partisan attack, making it far harder to build consensus for legitimate accountability in the future.

The weaponization of impeachment is no longer limited to presidents. In recent years, efforts to impeach federal judges for making legally sound but politically unpopular rulings have become increasingly common. In 2023, Republican lawmakers in the House introduced articles of impeachment against a federal district judge who blocked an Alabama ban on gender-affirming care for minors, arguing that the judge had “abused the power of the bench” to advance a liberal agenda. In 2022, progressive Democrats introduced similar articles to impeach Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas over undisclosed gifts from a conservative donor, a move that even many legal experts dismissed as an overreach of the impeachment power. These efforts send a chilling message to the federal judiciary: that judges can face removal for rulings that displease the majority party, undermining the core constitutional principle of judicial independence, which requires that judges be able to make decisions based on the law, not political pressure.

The harms of a low-threshold impeachment process extend far beyond political theater. First, it undermines democratic legitimacy: impeachment allows a simple majority in the House, which may represent a minority of the national electorate, to launch formal proceedings against a president elected by a national majority, effectively allowing Congress to overturn an electoral outcome without a new vote. This erodes the fundamental principle that electoral change is the only legitimate way to replace a sitting president, turning impeachment into a tool for minority rule. Second, it chills effective governance: presidents may avoid enforcing legally required but politically controversial policies—such as civil rights protections, environmental regulations, or anti-trust enforcement—for fear of triggering a partisan impeachment push. Similarly, judges may avoid ruling in favor of legally meritorious but unpopular claims to avoid being targeted for removal, gutting the rule of law. Third, it fuels political violence: partisan impeachment efforts reinforce the belief among a leader’s base that the opposing party is acting illegitimately to remove a democratically elected official, radicalizing supporters and increasing the risk of political violence, as seen in the January 6 Capitol riot, which was fueled in part by Trump supporters’ belief that his two impeachments were illegitimate deep-state plots. Finally, it debases the process itself: when impeachment is used for partisan stunts, the public stops taking it seriously when a real abuse of power occurs. If a president were to accept bribes from a foreign power or obstruct a criminal investigation into their own conduct, large swathes of the public would dismiss the impeachment effort as just another partisan witch hunt, making it nearly impossible to build the consensus needed for removal.

Opponents of raising the impeachment threshold will argue that doing so would make it impossible to remove corrupt or abusive officials, even in the face of clear evidence of wrongdoing. This claim, however, is belied by U.S. history. Every legitimate impeachment effort in U.S. history has enjoyed broad, bipartisan support. The only president to resign under threat of impeachment, Richard Nixon, had overwhelming bipartisan support for removal in both the House and Senate: the House Judiciary Committee approved articles of impeachment with bipartisan majorities, and Senate Republican leaders informed Nixon that he had the support of more than two-thirds of the chamber for conviction. Under the proposed higher thresholds, Nixon’s impeachment would have easily cleared both bars, as there was widespread agreement across party lines that his conduct in covering up the Watergate break-in constituted an impeachable abuse of power. For officials who commit actual crimes, criminal prosecution after leaving office remains a powerful check, and the risk of prosecution would still deter the vast majority of abuse. The proposed thresholds do not eliminate impeachment—they simply ensure it is reserved for the most serious, unambiguous cases of abuse, rather than being used as a partisan toy.

Another counterargument is that amending the Constitution to raise the threshold is too difficult, given the onerous requirements of two-thirds majorities in both houses of Congress and ratification by three-quarters of the states. But this is a feature, not a bug: the amendment process is deliberately designed to require broad, national consensus, which is exactly the standard that should apply to a process as grave as removing a federal official from office. The risk to the constitutional system from continued partisan weaponization of impeachment is far greater than the effort required to pass a targeted, narrowly tailored amendment. The Framers themselves expected that the Constitution would be amended to address unforeseen abuses, and the weaponization of impeachment is exactly the kind of unforeseen crisis the amendment process was designed to fix.

Impeachment is a core constitutional safeguard, but it only works if it is perceived as a legitimate, non-partisan check on abuse of power, not a tool for political gain. For over two decades, both parties have treated impeachment as a way to score points rather than uphold the Constitution, eroding public trust in the process and putting the entire system of checks and balances at risk. Raising the constitutional threshold for removal, as proposed, aligns the process with the Framers’ original intent, ensures that impeachment is reserved for the most serious cases of official misconduct, and protects against the partisan misuse that has come to define modern American politics. It is not a radical change: it is a return to the vision the Framers had when they wrote the impeachment clauses into the Constitution, a vision of a process that protects the republic from abuse, rather than being used to tear it apart for partisan gain.

Context: Current U.S. Impeachment Framework

Under the U.S. Constitution, impeachment of federal civil officials (including the president, vice president, federal judges, and cabinet secretaries) is governed by strict baseline rules:

  • The House of Representatives may vote to impeach (formally accuse) an official by a simple majority of members present.

Changes to these vote thresholds require a constitutional amendment (proposed by a two-thirds vote of both congressional chambers or a national convention, and ratified by three-fourths of state legislatures), a deliberately high bar. Procedural barriers (e.g., requirements for committee review, timelines for inquiries) may be modified via internal House or Senate rules, which each chamber sets for itself.

Proponents of raising impeachment thresholds or adding procedural barriers frame their arguments around three core goals: reducing partisan weaponization of the process, preserving stability of governance, and protecting constitutional checks and balances. The following are the stated rationales and purported benefits of these changes, as advanced by supporters of reform:

1. Mitigating Partisan Weaponization of Impeachment

The most widely cited rationale for raising barriers is to prevent impeachment from being used as a routine political weapon rather than a last-resort check on serious misconduct.

  • Under current rules, a political party with a narrow majority in the House can impeach a president, judge, or other official from the opposing party even with zero cross-party support. Proponents point to the largely party-line impeachments of Bill Clinton (1998), Donald Trump (2019 and 2021) as evidence that the current threshold enables purely partisan removals efforts focused on punishing political opponents rather than addressing egregious abuses of office.
  • Raising the House impeachment threshold (e.g., to a three-fifths or two-thirds supermajority) would require at least limited bipartisan support to advance articles of impeachment, eliminating frivolous, base-driven impeachments launched solely for political theater.
  • Procedural barriers (e.g., requiring a full House vote to authorize an impeachment inquiry, mandating bipartisan committee approval to advance articles of impeachment to the full chamber) would prevent single-party congressional leaders from launching investigations for partisan gain without colegislator buy-in.

Proponents argue these changes would restore the impeachment process as a non-partisan constitutional check, rather than a tool to score political points with a party’s base.

2. Preserving Stability of Executive and Judicial Functions

Impeachment is the only mechanism to remove a sitting president, vice president, or lifetime-tenured federal judge before their term ends. Proponents argue easy impeachment creates unnecessary instability in both branches:

  • For the executive, frequent or credible threats of partisan impeachment can disrupt a president’s ability to advance policy agendas, respond to crises, or carry out constitutionally mandated duties. A president may avoid enforcing lawful but politically controversial policies (e.g., environmental regulations, immigration enforcement) for fear of triggering a partisan impeachment, undermining the executive’s ability to function.
  • For the federal judiciary, lifetime tenure is explicitly designed to insulate judges from political pressure, allowing them to rule based on legal precedent rather than popular opinion. Proponents argue that easy impeachment removes this insulation, enabling the majority party in Congress to retaliate against judges for rulings they dislike, eroding judicial independence and the rule of law.
  • Higher barriers reduce the frequency of meritless impeachment threats, allowing officials to carry out their duties without constant fear of politically motivated removal, and preserving continuity of governance.

3. Ensuring Impeachment Is Reserved for Bipartisan-Validated Egregious Misconduct

The Constitution limits impeachment to “Treason, Bribery, or other high Crimes and Misdemeanors,” a standard intended to apply only to serious, extraordinary abuses of office, not policy disagreements or minor misconduct. Proponents of reform argue the current thresholds deviate from this intent:

  • A simple majority in the House can impeach an official for conduct that a large share of the public and Congress views as insufficient to warrant removal, eroding the legitimacy of the impeachment process as a whole. Recent impeachments have often been viewed by large swathes of the public as partisan overreaches, weakening the process’s reputation as a fair, serious check on power.
  • Higher thresholds force a broader, cross-party consensus that an official’s conduct rises to the level of removal, aligning the process with its original purpose as a rare, last-resort remedy for abuse of power. This, proponents argue, restores public trust in the process and ensures impeachment remains a tool for addressing genuinely extraordinary misconduct, not routine political disagreement.

4. Reducing Chilling Effects on Official Decision-Making

Proponents argue that the threat of easy, partisan impeachment creates a chilling effect on lawful official conduct:

  • Elected and appointed officials may avoid making lawful but politically controversial decisions to avoid angering the majority party in Congress. For example, a president may decline to enforce a federal law unpopular with the opposing party, or a federal judge may issue a legally incorrect ruling to avoid retaliatory impeachment.
  • Higher barriers reduce this risk by making clear that only conduct broadly condemned by both parties will lead to removal. This allows officials to act in accordance with their legal duties without fear of partisan retribution, upholding the integrity of executive and judicial decision-making.

5. Aligning Removal with National Consensus to Protect Democratic Outcomes

For elected officials like the president, impeachment overturns the outcome of a national election. For appointed officials like federal judges, it overturns the Senate’s advice and consent role in confirming nominees. Proponents argue a simple House majority is insufficiently representative to justify overturning these outcomes:

  • A simple majority in the House requires only 218 of 435 seats, which can represent as little as 17% of the U.S. population in low-turnout elections, and is often concentrated in a small number of gerrymandered districts. Proponents argue this narrow, potentially regionally concentrated majority should not have the power to remove a national leader or appointed official.
  • Raising thresholds ensures that a larger, more geographically and politically diverse coalition of lawmakers agrees removal is necessary, better reflecting broad national sentiment. This reduces the risk that a single party with a slim, polarized majority can remove an official disfavored by their base but supported by a large share of the country.

6. Reducing Waste of Legislative Resources

Under current rules, a partisan majority can impeach an official even if there is no realistic chance of Senate conviction (which already requires a two-thirds supermajority, a very high bar even with a Senate majority).Proponents argue these futile, partisan impeachments waste significant legislative resources:

  • Impeachment inquiries and trials can consume months of congressional time, millions of dollars in investigation costs, and divert attention from legislative priorities such as infrastructure, healthcare, and economic policy.
  • Higher House thresholds would filter out impeachments with no bipartisan support and no chance of Senate conviction, ensuring Congress only dedicates time and resources to proceedings with a legitimate chance of addressing serious misconduct.

Important Context and Tradeoffs

These are all purported benefits claimed by proponents of higher impeachment barriers; empirical evidence for their impact is limited, as only a small number of impeachments have occurred in U.S. history, and the recent rise in partisan impeachments is a modern phenomenon. Common counterarguments to reform include that higher thresholds make it excessively difficult to remove a truly corrupt, abusive, or unfit official, as even widely condemned misconduct may not garner the two-thirds Senate support required for conviction under current rules. Additionally, the high bar for constitutional amendment makes changes to impeachment thresholds extremely rare, a feature proponents argue is intentional, as the impeachment power is a fundamental check on government abuse that should not be easily altered for partisan gain.

The framers of the Constitution envisioned impeachment as a rare and solemn undertaking, reserved for what Alexander Hamilton called "offenses which proceed from the misconduct of public men" that injure "society itself." When impeachment becomes too readily available as a political weapon, it inflicts profound damage on democratic governance. First, it systematically undermines the legitimacy of elections. This transforms every midterm election into a potential recall election, destabilizing the fixed terms that provide continuity and predictability in democratic systems.

Second, the constant threat of impeachment fundamentally alters executive behavior in destructive ways. The Case for a Three-Quarters Threshold

Raising the Senate conviction threshold from two-thirds to three-quarters would restore impeachment to its intended role as a consensus-based remedy for undeniable misconduct. This higher bar would ensure that removal occurs only when wrongdoing is so manifest that it transcends partisan divisions. Protecting Democratic Stability

Frequent impeachment efforts create governmental instability that harms effective governance. Paradoxically, making impeachment more difficult would preserve its power. When impeachment becomes common, it loses its stigma and deterrent effect.   5. Revitalizing Public Trust in Government
    Finally, a more rigorous standard for impeachment can help restore public faith in government by mitigating the appearance—and sometimes the reality—of purely partisan motivations. Fortifying the Republic: The Case for Raising the Constitutional Threshold for Impeachment and Removal

Introduction

The impeachment mechanism enshrined in the United States Constitution represents one of the most consequential powers granted to the legislative branch—the authority to remove a sitting president, federal judge, or other civil officer from a position conferred either by national election or lifetime appointment. Yet what the Framers designed as a grave constitutional remedy reserved for extraordinary breaches of public trust has, in the modern era, drifted dangerously toward becoming another weapon in the arsenal of routine partisan warfare. The time has come for a serious national conversation about raising the constitutional threshold required for the removal of federal officials—moving beyond the current simple majority in the House for impeachment and two-thirds supermajority in the Senate for conviction—to a framework that demands even broader consensus before the republic resorts to overturning the results of democratic elections or disrupting the independent judiciary. Strengthening these barriers would not immunize corrupt officials from accountability; rather, it would restore impeachment to its proper constitutional stature, insulate the process from the most corrosive effects of polarization, and reinforce the structural principles of separation of powers and democratic legitimacy that undergird American self-governance.

I. The Framers' Intent and the Problem of Partisan Drift

To appreciate why a higher threshold is warranted, one must first understand the careful deliberation that produced the existing framework. The Constitutional Convention of 1787 debated impeachment extensively. The Framers were acutely aware of the English parliamentary tradition, in which impeachment had sometimes been wielded as a political bludgeon by factions seeking to destroy their rivals. Alexander Hamilton, writing in Federalist No. 65, acknowledged that impeachment trials "will seldom fail to agitate the passions of the whole community, and to divide it into parties more or less friendly or inimical to the accused." He warned that the process would inevitably "connect itself with the pre-existing factions, and will enlist all their animosities, partialities, influence, and interest on one side or on the other." Hamilton's prescience on this point has been vindicated by virtually every major impeachment proceeding in American history.

The Framers settled on the two-thirds requirement for Senate conviction precisely because they wanted to ensure that removal could not be accomplished by a narrow partisan majority. They understood that the graver the constitutional action, the broader the consensus it should require. Yet they could not have fully anticipated the depth of institutionalized partisanship that would emerge with the modern two-party system, the rise of nationalized media ecosystems that pressure legislators into lockstep party loyalty, or the extent to which the simple majority threshold for House impeachment would lower the initial barrier to launching proceedings motivated more by political calculation than genuine constitutional concern.

The trajectory of impeachment in recent decades illustrates the problem with painful clarity. In 1998, President Bill Clinton was impeached by a House divided almost entirely along party lines, with the proceedings widely perceived—even by many who found Clinton's behavior reprehensible—as driven substantially by partisan animus. In 2019 and 2021, President Donald Trump was impeached twice, again along largely partisan lines, with the first impeachment drawing not a single Republican vote in the House and the second drawing only ten. Regardless of where one stands on the merits of any of these cases, the pattern is unmistakable: impeachment has become a partisan exercise in which the majority party in the House can effectively place any president of the opposing party under the extraordinary stigma of impeachment with minimal cross-party support. This trend is corrosive to democratic norms and institutional legitimacy, and it will only accelerate unless structural barriers are erected against it.

II. The Democratic Legitimacy Argument

Perhaps the most powerful argument for raising the threshold concerns democratic legitimacy. A president of the United States is the only official elected by the entire national electorate. Tens of millions of citizens cast their votes to place that individual in office, and the mandate conferred by a national election represents the most direct expression of popular sovereignty in the American system. To nullify that mandate through impeachment and removal is, in effect, to override the collective judgment of the American people. Such an extraordinary act should require an extraordinary consensus among their representatives—a consensus even broader than what is currently mandated.

Under the present system, a simple majority of the House of Representatives—potentially representing as little as a narrow partisan faction—can initiate impeachment proceedings and formally impeach a president. While conviction requires two-thirds of the Senate, the impeachment itself carries enormous political and historical consequences: it consumes the government's attention for weeks or months, paralyzes policy-making, destabilizes financial markets, damages America's standing abroad, and permanently brands the accused official. The ease with which a House majority can inflict these costs creates a perverse incentive structure. When the House is controlled by the party opposing the president—a common occurrence in American politics—the temptation to weaponize impeachment for political advantage becomes nearly irresistible, particularly in an era when base mobilization and performative confrontation are rewarded by media attention and campaign donations.

Raising the House threshold to a supermajority—say, three-fifths or even two-thirds—would ensure that impeachment cannot proceed without substantial bipartisan support. This would mean that the initial decision to put the nation through the ordeal of an impeachment trial reflects a genuine, cross-partisan judgment that the official's conduct is so egregious as to warrant the most drastic constitutional remedy available. It would also protect the democratic choices of the electorate by ensuring that no narrow faction can unilaterally initiate the process of undoing a national election.

Similarly, raising the Senate conviction threshold—perhaps to three-fourths of senators present—would provide an even stronger guarantee that removal represents a true national consensus rather than a partisan majority supplemented by a handful of defectors from the other side. The logic is straightforward: the more consequential the action, the broader the agreement it should require. And there is no more consequential legislative action in the American system than removing a duly elected or appointed federal official from office.

III. Protecting Judicial Independence

The case for a higher threshold extends beyond the presidency to the federal judiciary, where the stakes for institutional integrity are arguably even greater. Federal judges serve lifetime appointments precisely to insulate them from political pressure, enabling them to render decisions based on law and constitutional principle rather than popular passion or partisan demand. The impeachment power, if too easily exercised, threatens to undermine this foundational principle of judicial independence.

In recent years, there have been increasing calls from partisans on both sides to impeach Supreme Court justices and lower federal judges whose rulings displease them. While such efforts have not yet succeeded, the mere threat of impeachment, if perceived as a realistic possibility achievable through partisan mobilization alone, can exert a chilling effect on judicial decision-making. A judge who knows that an unpopular but legally correct ruling could trigger impeachment proceedings backed by a simple House majority may, consciously or unconsciously, moderate decisions to avoid provoking legislative retaliation. This dynamic would gradually transform an independent judiciary into one responsive to political pressure—precisely the outcome the Framers sought to prevent through lifetime tenure.

Raising the threshold for impeachment and removal of federal judges would reinforce the structural independence of the judiciary by making clear that only the most extreme cases of misconduct—cases so egregious that they command near-unanimous agreement across party lines—can result in removal. Judges would be freed to exercise their constitutional judgment without fear that a transient partisan majority could end their careers for issuing disfavored rulings. The republic would be better served by a judiciary that answers to the Constitution rather than to the political winds of the moment.

IV. Reducing Institutional Damage and Governance Paralysis

Impeachment proceedings impose enormous costs on the nation's capacity for governance. When the House undertakes an impeachment inquiry, and especially when the Senate conducts a trial, the normal legislative business of the country grinds to a halt or is severely curtailed. Committee time, floor time, staff resources, and executive branch attention are all diverted from pressing policy matters—economic legislation, national security challenges, infrastructure investment, and countless other priorities that directly affect the lives of ordinary citizens.

These costs might be justified when impeachment addresses genuinely extraordinary misconduct. But when the process is initiated for primarily partisan reasons, the governance costs are imposed on the nation without corresponding benefit. The country suffers through months of political spectacle, only to arrive at a foreordained outcome in which the accused is acquitted along party lines, having been impeached along party lines. The net result is not accountability but dysfunction—a degradation of public trust in Congress, the presidency, and the constitutional system itself.

A higher threshold would serve as a natural filter, ensuring that impeachment proceedings are initiated only when there is sufficient bipartisan agreement that the matter is serious enough to justify the institutional costs. Frivolous or purely partisan impeachment efforts would be screened out at the earliest stage, preserving congressional resources and public attention for legitimate governance and for genuine cases of constitutional misconduct.

V. Addressing the Counterarguments

Critics of a higher threshold will raise several objections that deserve careful consideration.

The accountability objection. Some will argue that raising the threshold would make it effectively impossible to remove a corrupt or dangerous official, thereby creating impunity. This concern is understandable but ultimately overstated. Even under a higher threshold, removal would remain possible in cases of genuine, egregious misconduct—precisely the cases where broad bipartisan consensus would naturally emerge. The historical record suggests that when presidential misconduct is truly indefensible, members of the president's own party will break ranks. Richard Nixon resigned in 1974 not because the existing threshold was low but because his conduct was so clearly criminal that members of his own party informed him they could no longer defend him. A higher threshold would not have protected Nixon; it would merely have filtered out cases where the misconduct is ambiguous enough that reasonable people, unclouded by partisan loyalty, might disagree about whether it rises to the level warranting removal.

Moreover, impeachment is not the only mechanism of accountability. Criminal prosecution remains available for officials who commit actual crimes, either during or after their tenure. Electoral accountability provides a regular mechanism for voters to remove officials whose conduct they find unacceptable. Congressional oversight, public opinion, media scrutiny, and the political process itself all serve as checks on official misconduct. Impeachment was always intended to be a last resort, not a first-line mechanism of political accountability, and a higher threshold would restore it to that proper role.

The tyranny objection. Others will argue that a higher threshold could leave the nation vulnerable to a genuinely authoritarian president who, backed by a loyal partisan minority in the Senate, could not be removed regardless of conduct. This is a serious concern, but it must be weighed against the equally serious danger of a system in which impeachment becomes so routinized and politicized that it loses its moral authority entirely. A nation that impeaches presidents every few years along party lines will eventually find that impeachment carries no stigma, no deterrent effect, and no legitimacy—rendering it useless as a remedy even against genuine tyranny. By contrast, a system in which impeachment is rare, difficult, and commanding of broad consensus preserves the moral and political weight of the remedy, ensuring that when it is invoked, it carries the full force of national judgment.

Furthermore, the Constitution provides numerous other structural safeguards against tyranny: the separation of powers, federalism, an independent judiciary, the Bill of Rights, regular elections, civilian control of the military, and the amendment process itself. The impeachment mechanism is one thread in a rich tapestry of constitutional protections, and strengthening its threshold does not leave the nation defenseless against authoritarian overreach.

The originalism objection. Some constitutional scholars will argue that changing the impeachment threshold would betray the Framers' carefully calibrated design. But this objection conflates reverence for constitutional principles with rigid adherence to specific numerical thresholds. The Framers themselves provided the amendment process in Article V precisely because they recognized that the Constitution would need to evolve in response to unforeseen circumstances. The degree of institutionalized partisanship in modern American politics represents exactly such an unforeseen circumstance. The Framers chose the two-thirds threshold for Senate conviction at a time when political parties as we know them did not exist and when they could not have anticipated the iron discipline of modern party caucuses. Adjusting the threshold to account for this changed reality is not a betrayal of the Framers' vision but a faithful application of their underlying principle: that the most consequential constitutional actions should require the broadest possible consensus.

VI. The Structural Analogy

The logic of requiring supermajority consensus for the most consequential governmental actions is already well established in the American constitutional framework. Constitutional amendments require two-thirds of both chambers of Congress and ratification by three-fourths of the states. Treaty ratification requires two-thirds of the Senate. Overriding a presidential veto requires two-thirds of both chambers. These thresholds reflect the sound principle that actions of extraordinary consequence should not be achievable by narrow majorities. The removal of a federal official—particularly a president elected by the entire nation or a judge appointed for life—is at least as consequential as any of these actions and arguably more so. It would be entirely consistent with the structural logic of the Constitution to demand an even broader consensus for this most drastic of remedies than is currently required.

Consider the analogy to constitutional amendments. The Framers made the amendment process deliberately difficult, recognizing that changes to the fundamental law should not be made lightly or in response to transient passions. The same reasoning applies with equal force to impeachment, which effectively amends the outcome of a national election or a lifetime judicial appointment. If we require three-fourths of the states to agree before altering a provision of the Constitution, it is hardly unreasonable to require three-fourths of senators to agree before removing the head of a coequal branch of government.

VII. A Proposed Framework

While the specific numbers are subject to debate, a reasonable reformed framework might include the following elements:

  1. House impeachment threshold raised to two-thirds. This would ensure that no impeachment proceeds without substantial bipartisan support, filtering out purely partisan efforts at the earliest stage.

  2. Senate conviction threshold raised to three-fourths. This would guarantee that removal represents an overwhelming national consensus, not a partisan supermajority supplemented by a few crossover votes.

  3. A mandatory bipartisan composition requirement for impeachment inquiry committees, ensuring that the investigative process itself reflects cross-partisan participation from the outset.

These reforms would need to be implemented through the constitutional amendment process—itself a demanding undertaking that would require the very broad consensus the reforms seek to institutionalize. The difficulty of achieving such an amendment is not an argument against it; it is a feature that ensures the change itself commands the kind of national agreement it would subsequently demand of the impeachment process.

VIII. Conclusion

The impeachment power is a solemn constitutional trust. It exists not to provide partisan majorities with a mechanism for harassing political opponents but to protect the republic against genuine threats to constitutional governance. The increasing politicization of impeachment in the modern era threatens to strip this remedy of its moral authority, destabilize the democratic process, undermine judicial independence, and paralyze the government—all without producing meaningful accountability.

Raising the constitutional threshold for impeachment and removal would restore this extraordinary power to its intended purpose. It would ensure that the process commands genuine bipartisan consensus, protect the democratic choices of the electorate, reinforce the independence of the judiciary, and preserve the institutional legitimacy that makes impeachment meaningful. It would not create impunity for corrupt officials; rather, it would ensure that when the nation does resort to this most drastic of constitutional remedies, the judgment carries the full weight of a united republic rather than the hollow ring of a partisan vote.

The Framers gave us a constitutional system designed to resist the tyranny of faction. It is our responsibility to adapt that system to the realities of modern partisan politics, strengthening its safeguards where experience has shown them to be insufficient. Raising the impeachment threshold is not a retreat from accountability—it is an investment in the legitimacy, gravity, and effectiveness of the most powerful accountability mechanism the Constitution provides. The republic deserves nothing less than an impeachment process worthy of its seriousness.

We have watched the impeachment mechanism, that constitutional emergency brake designed for genuine crises of governance, slowly and steadily transformed into just another weapon in the partisan arsenal. Another tool of political warfare. Another cable news spectacle. Another fundraising email.

This is not what Hamilton envisioned when he warned us in Federalist 65 that impeachment trials would "seldom fail to agitate the passions of the whole community" and divide it along partisan lines. My friends, we have not been careful.

The Case for Higher Standards

Consider what we are truly saying when we impeach a federal official. We are saying to the millions of citizens who cast their votes, who stood in line, who exercised the most sacred right of a free people: "Your choice doesn't matter. Your voice is overruled. We in this chamber know better than you."

That is sometimes necessary. I will never deny that. There are genuine cases of treason, bribery, and profound abuses of power that demand removal. The Founders were not naïve—they knew that power corrupts, and they built this mechanism as a safeguard against tyranny.

But they also feared a different kind of tyranny—the tyranny of a legislature that could unseat the executive at will, reducing the President to a mere servant of congressional whim. They explicitly rejected the parliamentary model. They rejected "maladministration" as grounds for removal—James Madison himself struck it down at the Constitutional Convention because, as he argued, it would make the President serve at the pleasure of the Senate. They chose "high crimes and misdemeanors" precisely because they wanted a high bar. A very high bar.

Somewhere along the way, we lowered it. Not through amendment—oh no, we didn't have the courage or the honesty to do it through the proper channels. We lowered it through practice, through precedent, through the slow erosion of norms. We lowered it through the corrosive logic that says: if we have the votes, we have the justification.

I say: enough.

Let me tell you what happens when impeachment becomes routine—when it becomes expected, when it becomes the automatic response of any House majority that disagrees with the sitting president.

First, it paralyzes governance. An administration facing impeachment cannot govern. It cannot negotiate with foreign powers from a position of strength. It cannot advance domestic policy with focus and determination. Every official, every aide, every cabinet member is pulled into a defensive posture. The machinery of government grinds toward a halt—not because of any genuine crisis, but because of political theater.

Second, it poisons the well of democratic legitimacy. Every time we impeach along party lines—every time the vote breaks cleanly into red and blue—we tell the American people that this process is not about justice. It's about power. And we should not be surprised when they stop believing in the institutions we claim to protect.

Third, it creates an arms race. If one party impeaches when it holds the House, the other party will do the same when power shifts. And it always shifts. This is not hypothetical—we are living through this escalation right now. Each side points to the other's abuses to justify its own. And with every cycle, the bar drops lower, the justifications grow thinner, and the damage to our constitutional order deepens.

Fourth—and perhaps most dangerously—it discourages good people from serving. Who among us would submit ourselves, our families, our reputations to the meat grinder of a partisan impeachment? We are building a system that selects not for wisdom, integrity, or courage, but for the willingness to endure destruction. We will get the leaders we deserve if we make leadership unbearable for the leaders we need.

So what do I propose? I propose that we have the courage to do what the moment demands—to fortify the impeachment process against partisan abuse while preserving it as the vital safeguard it was designed to be.

First: Raise the threshold for impeachment in the House. A simple majority—a bare 218 votes—should not be sufficient to impeach a President of the United States and trigger the most consequential trial our government can conduct. I propose a supermajority requirement of three-fifths in the House to approve articles of impeachment. This single reform would accomplish what no amount of good faith and gentlemen's agreements has managed to achieve: it would require bipartisan consensus before the nation is put through the trauma of an impeachment trial. If a president's conduct is truly impeachable—truly rising to the level of high crimes—then surely members of both parties will recognize it. And if only one party sees fit to impeach? That is the very definition of partisan overreach.

Second: Establish a mandatory, independent preliminary inquiry. Before articles of impeachment are even drafted, an independent investigative body—composed of retired federal judges, former attorneys general, and distinguished legal scholars from across the political spectrum—should conduct a threshold review to determine whether the alleged conduct plausibly constitutes an impeachable offense under any reasonable constitutional interpretation. Their finding would not be binding—Congress must retain its constitutional prerogative—but it would serve as a check on impulsivity and a source of nonpartisan legal credibility. Third: Require specificity and evidentiary standards in articles of impeachment. No more vague, sweeping charges that amount to little more than political grievances dressed in legal language. Each article should be required to identify specific conduct, cite specific evidence, and articulate a specific constitutional basis for why that conduct meets the threshold of high crimes and misdemeanors. Between the introduction of articles and the vote on impeachment, there should be a mandatory period—I propose no less than 90 days—during which the House conducts its investigation, the accused mounts a defense, and the American people have time to weigh the evidence without the pressure of a rushed, politically timed vote. Impeachment should never be conducted on a legislative sprint. The gravity of the act demands deliberation, and deliberation demands time.

But the Founders also could not have foreseen a political landscape in which party loyalty overrides every other consideration, in which senators vote as blocks, and in which a two-thirds threshold can be reached through pure partisan alignment when one party holds a commanding majority. A three-fourths requirement would make removal truly extraordinary—an act of overwhelming national consensus rather than a strong partisan majority. It would preserve impeachment for the cases that truly demand it: the cases so egregious, so dangerous, so fundamentally threatening to the constitutional order that they unite the nation rather than divide it.

Answering the Critics

I reject every one of these charges.

I am not proposing the abolition of impeachment. I am proposing its preservation. Because a tool that is used for everything is a tool that means nothing. An impeachment process that is invoked every time the opposition wins the House is not a check on tyranny—it is tyranny wearing the mask of accountability.

The true friends of accountability are not those who would impeach at every opportunity. The true friends of accountability are those who would reserve this extraordinary power for extraordinary circumstances—and thereby ensure that when it is invoked, it carries the moral weight, the legal credibility, and the democratic legitimacy that the moment demands.

Think of it this way: we do not strengthen the fire alarm by pulling it every day. We strengthen it by ensuring that when it sounds, everyone takes it seriously.

We have the First Amendment and the right of the people to assemble and petition their government. Impeachment is not the only check on power—it is the last check on power. And last resorts must be treated as last resorts.

The Deeper Principle

My friends, there is a deeper principle at work here—one that transcends the mechanics of thresholds and timelines.

It is this: self-governance requires stability. Democracy is not merely the freedom to choose our leaders—it is the freedom to live under the leaders we have chosen until the next election gives us the opportunity to choose again. When we allow the impeachment process to become a shortcut around elections, we do not strengthen democracy. We subvert it. We tell the voters that their judgment is provisional, contingent, revocable—not by themselves at the ballot box, but by politicians in Washington.

The American people did not fight a revolution so that their chosen leaders could be removed by a partisan vote in Congress. They fought a revolution so that they, the people, would decide who governs. Every time we lower the bar for impeachment, we raise the bar for self-governance. Every time we make it easier to remove an official, we make it harder for the people's voice to endure.

I am not naive. I know that there will come a day—perhaps it has already come—when a president or a federal judge commits acts so egregious that removal is not merely justified but essential. For that day, we must preserve the power of impeachment in its full force and credibility. And the only way to do that is to stop spending that credibility on partisan vendettas.

A Call to Constitutional Courage

So I call on this body—I call on both parties—to rise above the temptation of the moment. I call on you to think not about the current occupant of the White House, whoever that may be, but about the office itself. Think about the next fifty years. Think about the precedents we are setting. Think about the nation we are building—or the nation we are unbuilding.

I call on you to have the constitutional courage to bind your own hands—to make it harder for yourselves to wield this awesome power, precisely because you know the temptation to wield it unwisely will always be there.

This is not weakness. This is the highest form of democratic strength. It is the recognition that in a republic, the greatest danger is not the tyrant who seizes power but the faction that wields legitimate power for illegitimate ends.

The Founders gave us impeachment as a shield against tyranny. Let us ensure it does not become a sword of faction.

Let us raise the standard. Let us fortify the process. Let us prove to ourselves and to the world that the American republic is strong enough, wise enough, and brave enough to protect its institutions—even from itself.

Thank you. And may God continue to bless the United States of America.

Strengthening the Impeachment Process: Safeguarding Democracy by Raising the Constitutional Threshold for Removal
